reminder: A 2-topos is a [2-category](c:2-category) that behaves like the 2-category of [2-sheaves](c:2-sheaf) on a [2-site](c:2-site).
definition: A (Grothendieck) 2-topos is a [2-category](c:2-category) that is equivalent to the 2-category of [2-sheaves](c:2-sheaf), that is category-valued sheaves, on a small [2-site](c:2-site). The 2-Giraud theorem describes these 2-categories by intrinsic exactness and generation properties, as Giraud's theorem does for a [Grothendieck topos](c:grothendieck-topos).
examples: The 2-category [Cat](c:cat) of small categories is a 2-topos: it is the 2-category of 2-sheaves on the one-point site.
For a small category $C$ with a topology, the 2-category of category-valued sheaves on $C$ is a 2-topos.
The 2-category of stacks of groupoids on a site is a (2,1)-topos, the case where every 2-cell is invertible.
Non-example: the 2-category of finite categories is not a 2-topos, because every 2-topos has all small 2-colimits and this one lacks infinite coproducts.

steps: Start with a [Grothendieck topos](c:grothendieck-topos) of set-valued sheaves on a site $C$.
Replace sets by categories and sheaves by [2-sheaves](c:2-sheaf), which glue objects and morphisms along covers.
A set is a discrete category, so the set-valued sheaves embed as the discrete 2-sheaves.
The 2-category of all 2-sheaves is the 2-topos of $C$, and the original topos sits inside it as its discrete objects.
links.why: It shows how the 2-topos of a site contains the ordinary topos of the same site as its discrete part.

reminder: An abelian differential graded Lie algebra is a [cochain complex](c:cochain-complex) with Lie bracket zero.
definition: A [differential graded Lie algebra](c:differential-graded-lie-algebra) $(L,d,[-,-])$ is abelian when its [Lie bracket](c:lie-bracket) satisfies $[x,y]=0$ for all $x,y\in L$. Then the bracket carries no information, so the data is just a [cochain complex](c:cochain-complex) $(L,d)$.
examples: Every cochain complex is one, for example the de Rham complex $\Omega^\bullet(M)$ with bracket $0$.
A vector space $V$ in degree $0$ with $d=0$ and bracket $0$ is an [abelian Lie algebra](c:abelian-lie-algebra), the degree-zero case.
Non-example: the forms $\Omega^\bullet(M,\mathfrak g)$ with values in a nonabelian Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ have the nonzero bracket $[\alpha\otimes x,\beta\otimes y]=\alpha\wedge\beta\otimes[x,y]$.

steps: Take a cochain complex $(V,d)$ and define the bracket by $[x,y]=0$.
Graded antisymmetry and the graded Jacobi identity hold, because every term is $0$.
The Leibniz rule $d[x,y]=[dx,y]\pm[x,dy]$ holds, because both sides are $0$.
So $(V,d,0)$ is a [differential graded Lie algebra](c:differential-graded-lie-algebra), and every abelian one arises in this way.
links.why: It shows that abelian differential graded Lie algebras are exactly the cochain complexes, so they need no new theory.

steps: Start with an [abelian Lie algebra](c:abelian-lie-algebra) $\mathfrak a$, a vector space with zero bracket.
Place $\mathfrak a$ in degree $0$ and set $d=0$.
The result is a cochain complex with zero bracket, so it is an abelian differential graded Lie algebra.
Conversely, such an algebra concentrated in degree $0$ with $d=0$ is an abelian Lie algebra.
links.why: It shows that the abelian Lie algebras are the degree-zero case of the graded and differential version.

reminder: A subgroup is an abelian normal subgroup when it is normal and any two of its elements commute.
definition: A [subgroup](c:subgroup) $A$ of a [group](c:group) $G$ is an abelian normal subgroup when $gAg^{-1}=A$ for every $g\in G$ and $ab=ba$ for all $a,b\in A$. Equivalently, $A$ is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of $G$ and an [abelian group](c:abelian-group).
examples: The center $Z(G)$ of any group $G$ is an abelian normal subgroup.
The Klein four-group $\{e,(12)(34),(13)(24),(14)(23)\}$ is an abelian normal subgroup of $S_4$.
The rotation subgroup of the dihedral group $D_n$ is cyclic and has index $2$, so it is an abelian normal subgroup.
Non-example: $A_4$ is normal in $S_4$ but not abelian, and $\langle(12)\rangle$ is abelian in $S_3$ but not normal.

steps: Let $A$ be an abelian normal subgroup of $G$.
By definition $A$ is closed under conjugation by every element of $G$, so it is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup).
The special case adds one condition: any two elements of $A$ commute.
links.why: It shows that every result about normal subgroups applies, and that commutativity is the only added condition.

steps: Take the [center](c:center) $Z(G)$, the set of elements that commute with all of $G$.
Conjugation by any $g\in G$ fixes each $z\in Z(G)$, so $Z(G)$ is normal.
Any two elements of $Z(G)$ commute, because each commutes with all of $G$.
So $Z(G)$ is an abelian normal subgroup.
links.why: It shows that the center is the standard source of abelian normal subgroups.

reminder: An actegory is a [category](c:category) on which a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) acts, up to coherent isomorphism.
definition: Let $(M,\otimes,I)$ be a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category). An $M$-actegory is a [category](c:category) $C$ with a [functor](c:functor) $\odot:M\times C\to C$ and [natural isomorphisms](c:natural-transformation) $(m\otimes n)\odot c\cong m\odot(n\odot c)$ and $I\odot c\cong c$. These isomorphisms satisfy pentagon and triangle laws that mirror those of $M$.
examples: Every monoidal category $M$ is an $M$-actegory over itself, with $\odot=\otimes$.
A cocomplete category $C$ is a $(\mathbf{Set},\times)$-actegory through copowers, $S\odot c=\coprod_{s\in S}c$.
The monoidal category of endofunctors $[C,C]$ acts on $C$ by evaluation, $F\odot c=F(c)$.
Non-example: the functor $m\odot c=c\times c$ on $\mathbf{Set}$ ignores $m\in(\mathbf{Set},\times)$ and gives $1\odot c=c\times c$, which is not naturally isomorphic to $c$.

steps: Let $(M,\otimes,I)$ be a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category).
Take $C=M$ and define the action by $m\odot c=m\otimes c$.
The associator and the left unitor of $M$ are the action isomorphisms, and the pentagon and triangle laws of $M$ give their coherence.
So every monoidal category is an actegory over itself.
links.why: It shows that an actegory extends a monoidal category to an action on a second category.

steps: Take a [module category](c:module-category): a linear category $C$ with an action of a tensor linear category $M$.
Forget the linear structure and keep the functor $M\times C\to C$ with its action isomorphisms.
The pentagon and triangle laws are unchanged.
So $C$ is an actegory over the underlying monoidal category of $M$.
links.why: It shows that a module category is an actegory in the linear setting.

reminder: A cancellative commutative additive monoid is a commutative monoid in which $a+b=a+c$ implies $b=c$.
definition: A [commutative monoid](c:add-comm-monoid) $(M,+,0)$ is cancellative when $a+b=a+c$ implies $b=c$ for all $a,b,c\in M$. Because $+$ is commutative, cancellation on the left and on the right are equivalent, so this is a [left-cancellative](c:add-left-cancel-monoid) monoid that is commutative.
examples: The natural numbers $(\mathbb{N},+,0)$ form one: $a+b=a+c$ gives $b=c$.
Every abelian group, such as $(\mathbb{Z},+)$, is one: add $-a$ to both sides.
The nonnegative reals $([0,\infty),+)$ form one.
Non-example: $(\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\},+)$ is a commutative monoid, but $1+\infty=2+\infty$ with $1\ne2$.

steps: Start with a [commutative monoid](c:add-comm-monoid) $M$.
Add the condition that $a+b=a+c$ implies $b=c$ for all $a,b,c$.
Then $M$ is a cancellative commutative additive monoid.
links.why: It shows that cancellation is the only extra condition over a commutative monoid.

steps: Let $G$ be an [abelian group](c:abelian-group), written additively.
If $a+b=a+c$, add $-a$ to both sides to get $b=c$.
So $G$ is cancellative, and with its zero it is a commutative monoid.
Hence every abelian group is a cancellative commutative additive monoid.
links.why: It shows that this concept keeps cancellation from abelian groups and drops the need for inverses.

reminder: The adelic group of a linear algebraic group $G$ is the [restricted product](c:restricted-product) of the groups $G(F_v)$ over all places $v$.
definition: Let $G$ be a [linear algebraic group](c:linear-algebraic-group) over a [number field](c:number-field) $F$. The adelic group $G(\mathbb{A}_F)$ is the [restricted product](c:restricted-product) of the locally compact groups $G(F_v)$ over all places $v$ of $F$, taken with respect to the compact open subgroups $G(\mathcal{O}_v)$ at almost all finite places. It is a locally compact [topological group](c:topological-group) that contains $G(F)$ as a discrete subgroup.
examples: For $G=\mathbb{G}_m$ the adelic group is the [group of ideles](c:group-of-ideles) $\mathbb{A}_F^\times$.
For $G=\mathrm{GL}_n$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, an element is a family $(g_v)$ with $g_v\in\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Z}_p)$ for almost all primes $p$.
For $G=\mathbb{G}_a$ the adelic group is the additive group of the [adeles](c:adele) $\mathbb{A}_F$.
Non-example: the full product $\prod_v G(F_v)$ is not the adelic group, because it allows $g_v\notin G(\mathcal{O}_v)$ for infinitely many $v$.

steps: Take $G=\mathbb{G}_m$, so that $G(F_v)=F_v^\times$ and $G(\mathcal{O}_v)=\mathcal{O}_v^\times$.
The restricted product of the groups $F_v^\times$ with respect to $\mathcal{O}_v^\times$ is the group of ideles.
So the [group of ideles](c:group-of-ideles) is the adelic group of $\mathbb{G}_m$.
links.why: It shows that the ideles are the first case of the adelic group construction.

steps: Take $G=\mathbb{G}_a$, so that $G(F_v)=F_v$ and $G(\mathcal{O}_v)=\mathcal{O}_v$.
The restricted product of the fields $F_v$ with respect to the rings $\mathcal{O}_v$ is the ring of adeles.
So the additive group of the [adeles](c:adele) is the adelic group of $\mathbb{G}_a$.
links.why: It shows that the adeles are the additive case of the adelic group construction.

reminder: An adiabatic invariant is a quantity that stays nearly constant when a parameter of the system changes slowly.
definition: Consider a [Hamiltonian](c:hamiltonian) system $H(q,p;\lambda)$ whose parameter changes slowly, $\lambda=\lambda(\varepsilon t)$ with $\varepsilon$ small. A function $I(q,p;\lambda)$ is an adiabatic invariant when, along solutions of [Hamilton's equations](c:hamilton-s-equations), its total change over times of order $1/\varepsilon$ tends to $0$ as $\varepsilon\to0$.
examples: For a [harmonic oscillator](c:harmonic-oscillator) with slowly changing frequency $\omega$, the ratio $E/\omega$ of energy to frequency is an adiabatic invariant.
For a system with one degree of freedom, the action $\oint p\,dq$ over one period is an adiabatic invariant.
The magnetic moment of a charged particle in a slowly varying magnetic field is an adiabatic invariant.
Non-example: the energy $E$ of the oscillator is not an adiabatic invariant, because $E$ changes in proportion to $\omega$ when $\omega$ changes.

reminder: An admissible set is a [transitive set](c:transitive-set) whose structure under membership satisfies Kripke-Platek set theory.
definition: A [transitive set](c:transitive-set) $A$ is admissible when $(A,\in)$ satisfies the axioms of Kripke-Platek set theory: extensionality, foundation, pairing, union, $\Delta_0$-separation and $\Delta_0$-collection. An [ordinal](c:ordinal) $\alpha$ is admissible when the set $L_\alpha$ of the [constructible universe](c:constructible-universe) is admissible.
examples: The set $\mathrm{HF}=L_\omega$ of [hereditarily finite sets](c:hereditarily-finite-set) is admissible.
The set $L_{\omega_1^{CK}}$ is admissible, where $\omega_1^{CK}$ is the least non-recursive ordinal.
The set $H(\omega_1)$ of hereditarily countable sets is admissible, because it satisfies even ZFC without the power set axiom.
Non-example: $L_{\omega+\omega}$ is transitive but not admissible, because $n\mapsto\omega+n$ is a $\Sigma_1$-definable map on $\omega$ with unbounded range, which violates collection.

steps: Take an admissible set $A$.
By definition $A$ is a [transitive set](c:transitive-set).
The special case adds one condition: $(A,\in)$ satisfies Kripke-Platek set theory, so it is closed under $\Delta_0$-separation and $\Delta_0$-collection.
links.why: It shows that admissibility is transitivity plus the weak closure properties of Kripke-Platek set theory.

reminder: The Albanese variety of a pointed variety $X$ is the universal [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety) that receives a basepoint-preserving map from $X$.
definition: Let $X$ be a smooth [projective variety](c:projective-variety) with a base point $x_0$. Its Albanese variety $\mathrm{Alb}(X)$ is an [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety) with a morphism $\mathrm{alb}:X\to\mathrm{Alb}(X)$ that sends $x_0$ to $0$ and has this [universal property](c:universal-property): every morphism from $X$ to an abelian variety $B$ that sends $x_0$ to $0$ factors as $\mathrm{alb}$ followed by a unique group homomorphism $\mathrm{Alb}(X)\to B$.
examples: For a smooth projective curve $C$, $\mathrm{Alb}(C)$ is its [Jacobian variety](c:jacobian-variety), and $\mathrm{alb}$ is the Abel-Jacobi map.
For an abelian variety $A$ with base point $0$, $\mathrm{Alb}(A)=A$ and $\mathrm{alb}$ is the identity.
For projective space $\mathbb{P}^n$, $\mathrm{Alb}(\mathbb{P}^n)$ is a point, because every morphism from $\mathbb{P}^n$ to an abelian variety is constant.
Non-example: for an elliptic curve $E$, the map $E\to E\times E$, $x\mapsto(x,0)$ is not an Albanese map, because homomorphisms $E\times E\to B$ that agree on $E\times0$ are not unique.

steps: Let $C$ be a smooth projective curve with base point $x_0$, and let $J(C)$ be its [Jacobian variety](c:jacobian-variety) with the Abel-Jacobi map $C\to J(C)$.
Every map from $C$ to an abelian variety that sends $x_0$ to $0$ factors uniquely through $J(C)$ by a homomorphism.
So $J(C)$ has the defining property of $\mathrm{Alb}(C)$.
Hence the Albanese variety of a curve is its Jacobian.
links.why: It shows that the Albanese variety extends the Jacobian from curves to higher-dimensional varieties.

reminder: Two different positive integers are amicable when each one equals the sum of the proper divisors of the other.
definition: Let $s(n)=\sigma(n)-n$ be the sum of the proper divisors of $n$, where $\sigma$ is the [divisor function](c:divisor-function). Two distinct [natural numbers](c:natural-number) $m$ and $n$ are amicable when $s(m)=n$ and $s(n)=m$.
examples: The pair $(220,284)$ is amicable: the proper divisors of $220$ sum to $284$, and those of $284$ sum to $220$.
The pair $(1184,1210)$ is the second smallest amicable pair.
Non-example: the number $6$ is not in an amicable pair, because $s(6)=6$ makes it a [perfect number](c:perfect-number), and the two numbers of a pair must differ.

reminder: An associated bundle replaces the fiber of a [principal bundle](c:principal-bundle) with a $G$-space on which the structure group acts.
definition: Let $\pi:P\to X$ be a [principal bundle](c:principal-bundle) with a right action of a group $G$, and let $F$ be a space with a left [action](c:group-action) of $G$. The associated bundle is $P\times_G F=(P\times F)/G$, where $g\cdot(p,f)=(pg^{-1},gf)$, with projection $[p,f]\mapsto\pi(p)$. Its fibers are copies of $F$.
examples: The tangent bundle of an $n$-manifold $M$ is $\mathrm{Fr}(M)\times_{GL_n}\mathbb{R}^n$, associated to the frame bundle.
The Möbius band is associated to the double cover $S^1\to S^1$, with $G=\mathbb{Z}/2$ acting on $[-1,1]$ by $t\mapsto-t$.
Taking $F=G$ with the conjugation action, or $F=\mathfrak g$ with the adjoint action, gives a bundle of the type of an [adjoint bundle](c:adjoint-bundle).
Non-example: the product $P\times F$ itself is not the associated bundle, because its fibers are $G\times F$ and not $F$.

steps: Let $P$ be a principal $G$-bundle.
Let $G$ act on itself by conjugation, or on its Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ by the adjoint action.
Form the associated bundle $P\times_G F$ for this action.
The result is an [adjoint bundle](c:adjoint-bundle) of $P$.
links.why: It shows that the adjoint bundle is the associated bundle for the conjugation or adjoint action.

steps: Let $E\to X$ be a vector bundle of rank $n$, and let $P=\mathrm{Fr}(E)$ be its frame bundle with $G=GL_n(\mathbb{R})$.
Let $G$ act on $F=\mathbb{R}^n$ in the standard way.
The map $[(e_1,\dots,e_n),v]\mapsto\sum_i v_ie_i$ is well defined and identifies $P\times_G F$ with $E$.
So every [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) is an associated bundle of its frame bundle.
links.why: It shows that vector bundles are the associated bundles whose fiber is a vector space with a linear action.

reminder: The Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequence computes a generalized cohomology of a CW complex from its ordinary cohomology with coefficients in the coefficient groups.
definition: For a [generalized cohomology](c:generalized-cohomology) theory $E^\bullet$ and a [CW complex](c:cw-complex) $X$, the Atiyah-Hirzebruch [spectral sequence](c:spectral-sequence) has $E_2^{p,q}=H^p(X;E^q(\mathrm{pt}))$, where $H^p$ is [ordinary cohomology](c:ordinary-cohomology). It comes from the skeletal filtration of $X$ and converges to $E^{p+q}(X)$ when $X$ is finite dimensional.
examples: For ordinary cohomology $E=H\mathbb{Z}$, the coefficients vanish except $E^0(\mathrm{pt})=\mathbb{Z}$, so the sequence collapses at $E_2$.
For complex $K$-theory, $E_2^{p,q}=H^p(X;K^q(\mathrm{pt}))$ with $K^q(\mathrm{pt})=\mathbb{Z}$ for even $q$, and the first differential is $d_3=Sq^3_{\mathbb{Z}}$.
For stable cohomotopy, the sequence starts from $H^p(X;\pi^s_{-q})$, the cohomology with coefficients in the stable homotopy groups of spheres.
Non-example: the Serre spectral sequence of a fibration $F\to E\to B$ has $E_2^{p,q}=H^p(B;H^q(F))$ and depends on a fibration, so it is a different sequence.

steps: Filter the CW complex $X$ by its skeleta $X^0\subseteq X^1\subseteq\cdots$.
Apply $E^\bullet$ to the pairs $(X^p,X^{p-1})$ to get an exact couple.
The exact couple gives a [spectral sequence](c:spectral-sequence) with $E_1^{p,q}=E^{p+q}(X^p,X^{p-1})$.
Its $E_2$ page is $H^p(X;E^q(\mathrm{pt}))$, and it converges to $E^{p+q}(X)$.
links.why: It shows where the sequence comes from: the skeletal filtration of the space, with one cohomology theory applied to it.

reminder: A block is an indecomposable two-sided ideal summand of the [group algebra](c:group-algebra) of a finite group.
definition: Let $G$ be a [finite group](c:finite-group) and $k$ a field of characteristic $p>0$. A block of $G$ is a primitive [central](c:center) [idempotent](c:idempotent) $e$ of the [group algebra](c:group-algebra) $kG$, that is, a nonzero central idempotent that is not a sum of two orthogonal nonzero central idempotents. The algebra $kG$ is the direct product of the algebras $kGe$ for its blocks $e$.
examples: If $p$ does not divide $|G|$, then $kG$ is semisimple and its blocks are its simple factors.
If $G$ is a $p$-group, then $kG$ has exactly one block, the principal block.
For $G=S_3$ and $p=2$, $kG\cong kC_2\times M_2(k)$ has two blocks.
Non-example: the identity $1$ of $kS_3$ for $p=2$ is a central idempotent but not a block, because $1=e_1+e_2$ with $e_1,e_2$ orthogonal central idempotents.

steps: Take a block $e$ of $kG$.
It is an [idempotent](c:idempotent), so $e^2=e$.
The special case adds that $e$ is central, so it commutes with every element of $kG$.
It also adds that $e$ is primitive: it is not a sum of two orthogonal nonzero central idempotents.
links.why: It shows that block theory studies one special family of idempotents of the group algebra.

reminder: A Brown functor is a contravariant set-valued functor that sends coproducts to products and homotopy pushouts to weak pullbacks.
definition: Let $\mathcal C$ be a [locally presentable (∞,1)-category](c:locally-presentable-infinity-1-category) with [homotopy category](c:homotopy-category-of-an-infinity-1-category) $\mathrm{Ho}(\mathcal C)$. A [functor](c:functor) $F:\mathrm{Ho}(\mathcal C)^{op}\to\mathbf{Set}$ is a Brown functor when it sends [coproducts](c:coproduct) to products and [homotopy pushouts](c:homotopy-pushout) to weak pullbacks. The second condition means that for a homotopy pushout square the map $F(B\sqcup_A C)\to F(B)\times_{F(A)}F(C)$ is surjective.
examples: Every representable functor $[-,Y]$ on the homotopy category is a Brown functor.
For a spectrum $E$, the cohomology functor $X\mapsto E^n(X)$ on pointed CW complexes is a Brown functor.
Ordinary cohomology $X\mapsto H^n(X;A)$ on pointed CW complexes is a Brown functor.
Non-example: the constant functor with value $\mathbb{Z}$ is not a Brown functor on pointed spaces, because $F(X\vee Y)=\mathbb{Z}$ is not $F(X)\times F(Y)=\mathbb{Z}^2$.

steps: Take an object $Y$ and form the functor $[-,Y]=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ho}(\mathcal C)}(-,Y)$.
A map out of a coproduct is a family of maps out of the summands, so $[-,Y]$ sends coproducts to products.
A map out of a homotopy pushout is a compatible pair of maps up to homotopy, so $[-,Y]$ sends homotopy pushouts to weak pullbacks.
So every [representable functor](c:representable-functor) is a Brown functor, and Brown representability gives the converse.
links.why: It shows that a Brown functor is a representable functor up to the two exactness conditions, and that these conditions are enough to recover representability.

reminder: The Burnside category of a finite group $G$ has finite $G$-sets as objects and formal differences of spans of $G$-sets as morphisms.
definition: Let $G$ be a [finite group](c:finite-group). The objects of the Burnside category are the finite $G$-sets, that is, [finite sets](c:finite-set) with a $G$-action. A morphism $X\to Y$ is a formal difference of isomorphism classes of spans $X\leftarrow U\to Y$ of finite $G$-sets, so each hom-set is a [group completion](c:group-completion), and composition is the pullback of spans.
examples: For the trivial group, a morphism between two finite sets is a formal difference of spans of finite sets, and $\mathrm{End}(\ast)=\mathbb{Z}$.
The composite of $X\leftarrow U\to Y$ and $Y\leftarrow V\to Z$ is $X\leftarrow U\times_Y V\to Z$.
The endomorphism ring of the one-point $G$-set is the [Burnside ring](c:burnside-ring) $A(G)$.
Non-example: the category of finite $G$-sets with ordinary equivariant maps is not the Burnside category, because a map $U\to X$ gives no morphism $X\to U$, called a transfer.

steps: Take the one-point $G$-set $\ast$ as an object.
A span $\ast\leftarrow U\to\ast$ is just a finite $G$-set $U$, and composition multiplies: $U\times_\ast V=U\times V$.
Disjoint union gives the addition, and formal differences give negatives, so $\mathrm{End}(\ast)$ is a ring.
This ring is the [Burnside ring](c:burnside-ring) $A(G)$.
links.why: It shows that the Burnside ring is the endomorphism ring of the point in the Burnside category.

reminder: A Cartesian monoidal category is a monoidal category whose tensor product is the categorical product and whose unit is a terminal object.
definition: A [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) $(C,\otimes,I)$ is Cartesian when $X\otimes Y$ is a [product](c:product-category-theory) of $X$ and $Y$ in $C$ and $I$ is a [terminal object](c:terminal-object). In a category with finite products, the choice of a product for each pair and a terminal object always gives such a structure.
examples: $(\mathbf{Set},\times,\{\ast\})$ and $(\mathbf{Cat},\times,\mathbf{1})$ are Cartesian monoidal.
$(\mathbf{Top},\times,\{\ast\})$ is Cartesian monoidal.
Non-example: $(\mathbf{Vect}_k,\otimes_k,k)$ is monoidal but not Cartesian, because $V\otimes W$ is not the product $V\oplus W$ and $k$ is not terminal.

steps: Start with a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) $(C,\otimes,I)$.
Require that $\otimes$ is the categorical product.
Require that $I$ is a terminal object.
Then $(C,\otimes,I)$ is a Cartesian monoidal category.
links.why: It shows that Cartesian structure is a property of a monoidal structure, not extra data.

steps: Let $C$ be a [Cartesian closed category](c:cartesian-closed-category), so it has finite products and each $-\times X$ has a right adjoint.
The finite products give the Cartesian monoidal structure $(C,\times,1)$.
The right adjoints $(-)^X$ make this monoidal structure closed.
So a Cartesian closed category is a Cartesian monoidal category that is closed.
links.why: It shows that Cartesian closed categories are the Cartesian monoidal categories with exponentials.

reminder: Classical logic is the logic in which every [proposition](c:proposition) satisfies the [law of excluded middle](c:law-of-excluded-middle).
definition:
Classical logic is the system of reasoning, in propositional or first-order form, in which each [proposition](c:proposition) $P$ is either true or false. Its proofs may use the [law of excluded middle](c:law-of-excluded-middle) $P\vee
eg P$, which is equivalent to elimination of [double negation](c:double-negation), $
eg
eg P\Rightarrow P$.
examples:
Every instance of $P\vee
eg P$ is a theorem, and so is $
eg
eg P\Rightarrow P$.
Peirce's law $((P\Rightarrow Q)\Rightarrow P)\Rightarrow P$ is a theorem.
A proof by contradiction of $P$ assumes $\neg P$ and derives a [contradiction](c:contradiction), and it is valid.
Non-example: [intuitionistic logic](c:intuitionistic-logic) is not classical, because it does not prove $P\vee\neg P$ for every $P$.

steps: Start with [intuitionistic logic](c:intuitionistic-logic), which has all the usual rules except excluded middle.
Add the law $P\vee\neg P$ for every proposition $P$ as an axiom.
Every intuitionistic proof stays valid, and elimination of double negation now follows.
The result is classical logic.
links.why: It shows that classical logic is intuitionistic logic plus excluded middle, so classical results can be compared with intuitionistic ones.

reminder: A map between topological spaces is closed when the image of every closed set is closed.
definition: A function $f:X\to Y$ between [topological spaces](c:topological-space) is closed when $f(C)$ is a [closed set](c:closed-set) of $Y$ for every closed set $C$ of $X$. Many authors also require $f$ to be [continuous](c:continuous-function).
examples: Every continuous map from a [compact space](c:compact-space) to a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space) is closed.
The projection $X\times K\to X$ is closed when $K$ is compact.
The inclusion of a closed subspace is a closed map.
Non-example: the projection $\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}$ is not closed, because the closed set $\{xy=1\}$ has image $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$, which is not closed.

steps: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism), a continuous bijection with continuous inverse.
For a closed set $C\subseteq X$, the image $f(C)$ equals the preimage $(f^{-1})^{-1}(C)$.
The inverse $f^{-1}$ is continuous, so this preimage is closed.
So $f$ is a closed map.
links.why: It shows that a closed map keeps the part of a homeomorphism that sends closed sets to closed sets, with no inverse needed.

steps: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous [proper map](c:proper-map), where $Y$ is locally compact Hausdorff.
Let $C\subseteq X$ be closed and let $y$ lie in the closure of $f(C)$.
Choose a compact neighborhood $K$ of $y$; then $f(C)\cap K=f(C\cap f^{-1}(K))$ is compact, so it is closed in $Y$.
Since $y$ lies in the closure of $f(C)\cap K$, we get $y\in f(C)$, so $f(C)$ is closed.
links.why: It shows that proper maps into locally compact Hausdorff spaces are closed, so closedness is the weaker and more general property.

reminder: In a co-Heyting algebra, the negation $\sim a$ is the least element whose join with $a$ is the top element.
definition: In a [co-Heyting algebra](c:co-heyting-algebra) $H$, the co-Heyting negation of $a$ is $\sim a=1\setminus a$, where $b\setminus a$ is the least $c$ with $b\le a\vee c$. So $\sim a$ is the least element with $a\vee(\sim a)=1$. It satisfies the law of excluded middle but not always the law of non-contradiction, which is dual to the behavior of Heyting [negation](c:negation).
examples: In a Boolean algebra, $\sim a$ is the usual complement $\neg a$.
In the lattice of closed subsets of a space $X$, $\sim A$ is the closure of $X\setminus A$.
For $A=[0,1]\subset\mathbb{R}$, $\sim A=(-\infty,0]\cup[1,\infty)$, so $A\cap\sim A=\{0,1\}\ne\emptyset$ and non-contradiction fails.
Non-example: the Heyting negation $\neg a$ is the greatest element with $a\wedge\neg a=0$; it is the dual operation, not the co-Heyting negation.

reminder: The $n$th codimension of an algebra is the dimension of its multilinear polynomials of degree $n$ modulo its identities.
definition: Let $A$ be an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) over a field of characteristic $0$, and let $P_n$ be the space of multilinear polynomials in $x_1,\dots,x_n$ in the [free algebra](c:free-algebra). The codimension sequence of $A$ is $c_n(A)=\dim P_n/(P_n\cap\mathrm{Id}(A))$, where $\mathrm{Id}(A)$ is the set of [polynomial identities](c:polynomial-identity) of $A$. By Regev's theorem it is bounded by an exponential when $A$ is a [PI-algebra](c:pi-algebra).
examples: For a commutative algebra with $1$, such as $F[x]$, $c_n=1$ for all $n$.
For the Grassmann algebra $E$ on infinitely many generators, $c_n(E)=2^{n-1}$.
For the algebra $M_2(F)$ of $2\times2$ matrices, $c_n$ grows like $4^n$ up to a polynomial factor.
Non-example: the free algebra has no nontrivial identity and $c_n=n!$, which is not exponentially bounded, so no PI-algebra has this sequence.

reminder: A comonoid is an object with a coassociative comultiplication and a counit, the dual of a monoid object.
definition: A comonoid in a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) $(M,\otimes,I)$ is an object $C$ with morphisms $\Delta:C\to C\otimes C$ and $\varepsilon:C\to I$ such that $(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\Delta)\Delta$ and $(\varepsilon\otimes\mathrm{id})\Delta=\mathrm{id}=(\mathrm{id}\otimes\varepsilon)\Delta$, up to the associator and the unitors. Equivalently, it is a [monoid in a monoidal category](c:monoid-in-a-monoidal-category) in the [opposite category](c:opposite-category) $M^{op}$.
examples: In $(\mathbf{Set},\times,1)$ every set $X$ is a comonoid in exactly one way: $\Delta(x)=(x,x)$ and $\varepsilon$ is the map to $1$.
In $(\mathrm{Vect}_k,\otimes)$ a comonoid is a [coalgebra](c:coalgebra); for a set $S$ the space $k[S]$ has $\Delta(s)=s\otimes s$ and $\varepsilon(s)=1$.
For a finite-dimensional algebra $A$, the dual space $A^*$ is a comonoid in $\mathrm{Vect}_k$.
Non-example: for a nonzero vector space $V$, the zero maps $\Delta=0$ and $\varepsilon=0$ are not a comonoid structure, because the counit law would give $\mathrm{id}_V=0$.

steps: Take the monoidal category $(\mathrm{Vect}_k,\otimes_k,k)$ of vector spaces over a field $k$.
A comonoid in it is a vector space $C$ with $\Delta:C\to C\otimes C$ and $\varepsilon:C\to k$.
Coassociativity and the counit laws are the axioms of a [coalgebra](c:coalgebra).
So a coalgebra is a comonoid in $\mathrm{Vect}_k$.
links.why: It shows that coalgebras are one case of comonoids, so results for comonoids apply to them.

reminder: Two sequences of positive integers are complementary when every positive integer occurs in exactly one of them.
definition: Two strictly increasing [sequences](c:sequence) $(a_n)$ and $(b_n)$ of positive integers are complementary when every positive integer is a term of exactly one of them. In other words, the sets $\{a_n\}$ and $\{b_n\}$ are disjoint and their union is the set of positive [natural numbers](c:natural-number).
examples: The odd and the even positive integers are complementary.
The squares $n^2$ and the non-squares $n+\lfloor\sqrt n+\tfrac12\rfloor$ are complementary.
The Beatty sequences $\lfloor n\alpha\rfloor$ and $\lfloor n\beta\rfloor$ are complementary when $\alpha,\beta>1$ are irrational and $1/\alpha+1/\beta=1$.
Non-example: the even numbers and the multiples of $3$ are not complementary, because $6$ lies in both and $1$ lies in neither.

reminder: A metric space is complete when every [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) in it converges to a point of the space.
definition: A [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$ is complete when every [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) in $X$ converges to a point of $X$. A normed space that is complete in its norm metric is a [Banach space](c:banach-space). An orthonormal system in a Hilbert space is also called complete when only the zero vector is orthogonal to all its members.
examples: $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$ are complete, and so is every closed subset of a complete metric space.
The space $L^2([0,1])$ is complete, and $\{e^{2\pi inx}\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}$ is a complete orthonormal system in it.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Q}$ with the usual metric is not complete, because the decimal truncations of $\sqrt2$ form a Cauchy sequence with no limit in $\mathbb{Q}$.

steps: Let $X$ be a [Banach space](c:banach-space), a normed vector space that is complete in its norm.
The norm gives the metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$.
Completeness of $X$ says that every Cauchy sequence for this metric converges.
So $X$ is a complete metric space with extra linear structure.
links.why: It shows that a Banach space is a normed space that has the completeness property.

steps: Let $X$ be a [compact space](c:compact-space) with a metric, and let $(x_n)$ be a Cauchy sequence in $X$.
By compactness, some subsequence converges to a point $x\in X$.
A Cauchy sequence with a convergent subsequence converges to the same limit.
So $X$ is complete.
links.why: It shows that for metric spaces compactness is a stronger property than completeness.

reminder: A complex analytic space is locally the common zero set of finitely many holomorphic functions, with the induced sheaf of functions.
definition: A complex analytic space is a [locally ringed space](c:locally-ringed-space) $(X,\mathcal{O}_X)$, with $X$ Hausdorff, such that every point has an open neighborhood isomorphic to a local model. A local model is the zero set $Z=V(f_1,\dots,f_k)$ of finitely many [holomorphic functions](c:holomorphic-function) on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb{C}^n$, with the [structure sheaf](c:structure-sheaf) $(\mathcal{O}_U/(f_1,\dots,f_k))|_Z$.
examples: Every [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) is one, with $k=0$ in every local model.
The cusp $\{y^2=x^3\}\subset\mathbb{C}^2$ and the node $\{xy=0\}\subset\mathbb{C}^2$ are complex analytic spaces with [singularities](c:singularity).
The double point $\{x^2=0\}\subset\mathbb{C}$, with structure sheaf $\mathcal{O}/(x^2)$, is a nonreduced complex analytic space.
Non-example: the closed disc $\{|z|\le1\}\subset\mathbb{C}$ is not one, because its boundary points have no neighborhood isomorphic to a local model.

steps: Let $M$ be a [complex manifold](c:complex-manifold) of dimension $n$.
Each point has a chart onto an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb{C}^n$, with holomorphic transition maps.
This chart is a local model with no equations, $k=0$, and with structure sheaf $\mathcal{O}_U$.
So $M$ is a complex analytic space, and the manifolds are the smooth ones.
links.why: It shows that complex analytic spaces allow singular points where a complex manifold does not.

steps: Take an [analytic space](c:analytic-space) over the complete valued field $\mathbb{C}$ with its usual absolute value.
Convergent power series over $\mathbb{C}$ in $n$ variables are the germs of holomorphic functions on $\mathbb{C}^n$.
The local models become zero sets of holomorphic functions with the quotient structure sheaf.
So analytic spaces over $\mathbb{C}$ are the complex analytic spaces.
links.why: It shows that the complex case of analytic spaces is the one that uses holomorphic functions.

reminder: Complex conjugation sends $a+bi$ to $a-bi$, so it reverses the sign of the imaginary part.
definition: Complex conjugation is the [function](c:function) $\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ that sends $z=a+bi$, with $a,b$ real, to $\bar z=a-bi$. It fixes exactly the real numbers, satisfies $\bar{\bar z}=z$, and obeys $\overline{z+w}=\bar z+\bar w$ and $\overline{zw}=\bar z\bar w$ on the [complex numbers](c:complex-number).
examples: $\overline{3+4i}=3-4i$, and $z\bar z=|z|^2$ for every $z$.
If $p$ has real coefficients and $p(z)=0$, then $p(\bar z)=0$.
Non-example: the map $z\mapsto-z$ is not complex conjugation, because it also negates the real part and so fixes no nonzero real number.

steps: Check that $z\mapsto\bar z$ is additive and multiplicative, with $\bar1=1$.
It is its own inverse, so it is a bijection of $\mathbb{C}$.
A bijection that preserves sum, product and $1$ is an [automorphism of the complex numbers](c:automorphism-of-the-complex-numbers).
It is the only continuous automorphism of $\mathbb{C}$ other than the identity.
links.why: It shows that complex conjugation is the one nontrivial continuous field automorphism of the complex numbers.

steps: Apply conjugation twice: $\bar{\bar z}=z$ for every $z$.
So the composite of conjugation with itself is the identity map.
A map that is its own inverse is an [involution](c:involution).
links.why: It shows that conjugation is an involution, so it splits $\mathbb{C}$ into real and imaginary parts.

reminder: The complex projective plane $\mathbb{C}P^2$ is the space of complex lines through the origin in $\mathbb{C}^3$.
definition: The complex projective plane is $\mathbb{C}P^2=(\mathbb{C}^3\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb{C}^\times$, the set of complex lines through $0$ in $\mathbb{C}^3$, with homogeneous coordinates $[z_0:z_1:z_2]$. It is the [complex projective space](c:complex-projective-space) of complex dimension $2$ and the [projective plane](c:projective-plane) over the [complex numbers](c:complex-number); it is a compact complex manifold of real dimension $4$.
examples: The chart $z_0\ne0$ identifies a dense open subset of $\mathbb{C}P^2$ with $\mathbb{C}^2$, and the line $z_0=0$ is a copy of $\mathbb{C}P^1$ at infinity.
Its cohomology ring is $\mathbb{Z}[x]/(x^3)$ with $|x|=2$, and it has one cell in each of the dimensions $0$, $2$ and $4$.
Two distinct lines in $\mathbb{C}P^2$ meet in exactly one point.
Non-example: $\mathbb{C}P^1\times\mathbb{C}P^1$ is also a compact complex surface, but it is not $\mathbb{C}P^2$, because its $H^2$ has rank $2$ and $H^2(\mathbb{C}P^2)$ has rank $1$.

steps: [Complex projective space](c:complex-projective-space) $\mathbb{C}P^n$ is the set of complex lines through $0$ in $\mathbb{C}^{n+1}$.
Choose $n=2$.
The lines through $0$ in $\mathbb{C}^3$ form $\mathbb{C}P^2$, a space of complex dimension $2$.
links.why: It shows that the complex projective plane is the two-dimensional case of complex projective space.

steps: A [projective plane](c:projective-plane) over a field $K$ has as points the lines through $0$ in $K^3$, and as lines the planes through $0$.
Take $K=\mathbb{C}$.
Two points lie on one line and two lines meet in one point, as in every projective plane.
links.why: It shows that the complex projective plane is the projective plane over the complex numbers.

reminder: The configuration space of $n$ points in $X$ is the space of $n$-tuples of pairwise distinct points of $X$.
definition: For a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ and $n\ge1$, the configuration space is $\mathrm{Conf}_n(X)=\{(x_1,\dots,x_n)\in X^n:x_i\ne x_j\text{ for }i\ne j\}$, with the subspace topology of the [product topology](c:product-topology) on $X^n$. The symmetric group $S_n$ acts on it by permuting coordinates, and the quotient is the unordered configuration space.
examples: $\mathrm{Conf}_2(\mathbb{R}^m)$ is homotopy equivalent to the sphere $S^{m-1}$, by sending $(x,y)$ to $(x-y)/|x-y|$.
$\mathrm{Conf}_n(\mathbb{R})$ has $n!$ components, one for each ordering of the points, and each is contractible.
The fundamental group of $\mathrm{Conf}_n(\mathbb{C})$ is the pure braid group, a subgroup of the [braid group](c:braid-group).
Non-example: the product $X^n$ is not $\mathrm{Conf}_n(X)$, because it allows two points to coincide; the symmetric product $X^n/S_n$ allows this too and forgets the order.

reminder: A conformal compactification embeds a non-compact Lorentzian manifold conformally as a dense open subset of a compact one.
definition: A conformal compactification of a non-compact [Lorentzian manifold](c:lorentzian-manifold) $(M,g)$ is a compact Lorentzian manifold $(\hat M,\hat g)$ with an [embedding](c:embedding) $\iota:M\to\hat M$ onto a [dense](c:dense-subspace) open subset, such that $\iota$ is a [conformal map](c:conformal-map), that is, $\iota^*\hat g=\Omega^2g$ for a positive smooth function $\Omega$.
examples: The conformal compactification of Minkowski space $\mathbb{R}^{1,3}$ is $(S^1\times S^3)/\mathbb{Z}_2$ with a conformally flat metric.
More generally, $\mathbb{R}^{1,d-1}$ has the conformal compactification $(S^1\times S^{d-1})/\mathbb{Z}_2$.
Non-example: the one-point compactification $\mathbb{R}^{1,3}\cup\{\infty\}\cong S^4$ is not one, because $S^4$ carries no Lorentzian metric.

steps: A [compactification](c:compactification) of a space $X$ is a compact space that contains $X$ as a dense subspace through an embedding.
Take $X$ to be a non-compact Lorentzian manifold and the compact space to be a Lorentzian manifold.
Require that the embedding is a conformal map, so it preserves the conformal class of the metric.
Then the compactification is a conformal compactification.
links.why: It shows that a conformal compactification is an ordinary compactification that also respects the Lorentzian conformal structure.

reminder: Conjugation of $h$ by $g$ in a group is the element $ghg^{-1}$.
definition: Let $G$ be a [group](c:group) and $g\in G$. Conjugation by $g$ is the map $c_g:G\to G$ with $c_g(h)=ghg^{-1}$. Each $c_g$ is an [automorphism](c:automorphism) of $G$, and $c_{gk}=c_g\circ c_k$.
examples: In $S_n$, conjugating the [cycle](c:cyclic-permutation) $(a_1\,a_2\,\dots\,a_k)$ by $\sigma$ gives the cycle $(\sigma(a_1)\,\sigma(a_2)\,\dots\,\sigma(a_k))$.
In $GL_n$, conjugation $A\mapsto PAP^{-1}$ is a change of basis.
In an abelian group, every conjugation $c_g$ is the identity.
Non-example: the map $h\mapsto ghg$ is not a conjugation, and it is not a homomorphism unless $g^2=e$, because it sends $e$ to $g^2$.

steps: Let $G$ act on the set $G$ by $g\cdot h=ghg^{-1}$.
The identity acts trivially, because $e\cdot h=h$.
The action is compatible with the product: $g\cdot(k\cdot h)=gkhk^{-1}g^{-1}=(gk)\cdot h$.
So conjugation is a [group action](c:group-action) of $G$ on itself, and each element acts by an automorphism.
links.why: It shows that conjugation is the action of a group on itself by automorphisms, so orbit and stabilizer results apply.

reminder: A constant function takes the same value at every point of its domain.
definition: A [function](c:function) $f:S\to T$ is constant when it takes one value on all of $S$: there is an element $x\in T$ with $f(a)=x$ for every $a\in S$. For a fixed $x$, the constant function with value $x$ is the map $a\mapsto x$.
examples: The function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ with $f(t)=5$ is constant, and its derivative is $0$ everywhere.
The unique function from any set $S$ to a one-point set is constant.
Non-example: the identity function on a set with at least two elements is not constant, because it takes different values at different points.

steps: In the category of sets, the terminal object is a one-point set $1$.
A [constant morphism](c:constant-morphism) $S\to T$ factors as $S\to1\to T$.
A map $1\to T$ picks one element $x\in T$.
The composite sends every $a\in S$ to $x$, so it is the constant function with value $x$.
links.why: It shows that constant functions are the constant morphisms of the category of sets.

reminder: A continuous extension of a continuous function on a subset is a continuous function on a larger set that agrees with it on the subset.
definition: Let $A\subseteq X$ be a subset of a [topological space](c:topological-space) and let $f:A\to Y$ be a [continuous function](c:continuous-function). A continuous extension of $f$ to $X$ is a continuous function $F:X\to Y$ with $F(a)=f(a)$ for every $a\in A$.
examples: The function $\sin(x)/x$ on $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ has a continuous extension to $\mathbb{R}$ that takes the value $1$ at $0$.
A uniformly continuous function from a dense subset of a metric space into a complete metric space has a unique continuous extension to the whole space.
By the Tietze theorem, every continuous real function on a closed subset of a normal space has a continuous extension.
Non-example: the function $\sin(1/x)$ on $(0,1]$ has no continuous extension to $[0,1]$, because its values near $0$ oscillate between $-1$ and $1$.

reminder: A covering sieve on an object is a sieve that belongs to the Grothendieck topology of the site.
definition: Let $(C,J)$ be a [Grothendieck site](c:grothendieck-site), that is, a category $C$ with a Grothendieck topology $J$. A covering sieve on an object $U$ is a [sieve](c:sieve) $S$ on $U$, a set of arrows into $U$ closed under precomposition, that belongs to $J(U)$. A family of arrows [covers](c:covering) $U$ when the sieve that it generates is a covering sieve.
examples: On the site of open sets of a space $X$, the sieve of all open $V\subseteq U$ that lie in some member of an open cover of $U$ is a covering sieve of $U$.
The maximal sieve of all arrows into $U$ is a covering sieve in every Grothendieck topology.
On an [atomic site](c:atomic-site), every nonempty sieve is a covering sieve.
Non-example: on the open sets of $\mathbb{R}$, the sieve of all $V\subseteq(0,1)$ on the object $(-1,1)$ is not a covering sieve, because its members do not cover $(-1,1)$.

steps: Start with a [sieve](c:sieve) $S$ on an object $U$ of a site.
Add the condition that $S$ belongs to the Grothendieck topology $J(U)$.
Then $S$ is a covering sieve.
links.why: It shows that being covering is the one extra property of a sieve, and the sheaf condition speaks only of those sieves.

reminder: The Cramér model treats each integer $n\ge3$ as prime with probability $1/\log n$, independently of the other integers.
definition: The Cramér model is a random set $R\subseteq\{3,4,\dots\}$ built from [independent](c:independence) [random variables](c:random-variable) $X_n$ with $P(X_n=1)=1/\log n$ and $P(X_n=0)=1-1/\log n$, where $\log$ is the [logarithm](c:logarithm). The integer $n$ lies in $R$ when $X_n=1$, and the elements of $R$ are the random primes that model the [prime numbers](c:prime-number).
examples: In the model, $|R\cap[1,x]|\sim x/\log x$ almost surely, in agreement with the prime number theorem.
Almost surely, the gaps between consecutive elements of $R$ are $O((\log n)^2)$, and this led Cramér to conjecture the same bound for the gaps between real primes.
Non-example: the set of real primes is not a typical sample of the model, because $n$ and $n+1$ are both prime only for $n=2$, but almost surely they both lie in $R$ for infinitely many $n$.

reminder: The cross section of a scattering process is the effective area that a target presents to a beam for that process.
definition: In scattering theory, the cross section $\sigma$ of a process is the effective [area](c:area) that one target particle presents to the incoming beam. The rate of the process equals $\sigma$ times the incident flux times the number of targets, so $\sigma$ has the dimension of an area.
examples: A point projectile that hits a hard sphere of radius $a$ has the total cross section $\pi a^2$.
Rutherford scattering of charged particles has a differential cross section proportional to $1/\sin^4(\theta/2)$.
The barn, equal to $10^{-28}\,\mathrm{m}^2$, is a unit of cross section.
Non-example: a cross section of a fiber bundle, a map that chooses one point in each fiber, is a different concept with the same name.

reminder: A cubic surface is the zero set in projective 3-space of one homogeneous polynomial of degree $3$.
definition: A cubic surface is the zero set $V(F)\subset\mathbb{P}^3$ of a nonzero [homogeneous polynomial](c:homogeneous-polynomial) $F$ of degree $3$ in four variables, where $\mathbb{P}^3$ is [projective space](c:projective-space) of dimension $3$. It is a [hypersurface](c:hypersurface) of degree $3$, and a smooth cubic surface over $\mathbb{C}$ contains exactly $27$ lines.
examples: The Fermat cubic $x^3+y^3+z^3+w^3=0$ is a smooth cubic surface with $27$ lines.
Cayley's nodal cubic surface $xyz+xyw+xzw+yzw=0$ has $4$ nodes.
Non-example: the quadric $xy=zw$ has degree $2$ and the quartic $x^4+y^4+z^4+w^4=0$ has degree $4$, so neither is a cubic surface.

steps: A [hypersurface](c:hypersurface) in $\mathbb{P}^n$ is the zero set of one nonzero homogeneous polynomial.
Take $n=3$, so the hypersurface has dimension $2$ and is a surface.
Take a polynomial of degree $3$.
The zero set is a cubic surface.
links.why: It shows that a cubic surface is the degree-3 hypersurface in projective 3-space.

reminder: A cycle decomposition of a graph splits its edge set into edge-disjoint cycles.
definition: A cycle decomposition of a [graph](c:graph) $G$ is a set of [cycles](c:cycle) of $G$ such that every edge of $G$ lies in exactly one of them. A graph has a cycle decomposition only if every vertex has even degree, and the decomposition has type $(k_1,\dots,k_m)$ when the cycle lengths are $k_1,\dots,k_m$.
examples: The complete graph $K_5$ decomposes into two $5$-cycles.
The complete graph $K_7$ decomposes into $7$ triangles, which are the lines of the Fano plane.
Non-example: $K_4$ has no cycle decomposition, because every vertex has degree $3$, which is odd.

reminder: The cyclic bar construction of a monoid $M$ is the cyclic object with $M^{n+1}$ in degree $n$ and a wrap-around last face.
definition: For a [monoid](c:monoid) $M$, the cyclic bar construction $B^{cy}M$ is the [cyclic object](c:cyclic-object) in sets with $B^{cy}_nM=M^{n+1}$. Its faces are $d_i(m_0,\dots,m_n)=(m_0,\dots,m_im_{i+1},\dots,m_n)$ for $i<n$ and $d_n(m_0,\dots,m_n)=(m_nm_0,m_1,\dots,m_{n-1})$. Its degeneracies insert the unit, and its cyclic operator rotates the entries.
examples: For a group $G$, the geometric realization of $B^{cy}G$ is homotopy equivalent to the [free loop space](c:free-loop-space) of the classifying space $BG$.
For an associative algebra $A$, the same formulas on the tensor powers $A^{\otimes(n+1)}$ give the complex that computes [Hochschild homology](c:hochschild-homology).
Non-example: the ordinary [bar construction](c:bar-construction) has $M^n$ in degree $n$ and no wrap-around face $d_n$, so it is not a cyclic object.

reminder: A functor is a dense subsite when restriction along it gives an equivalence between the categories of sheaves.
definition: A [functor](c:functor) $G:C\to D$ between small [Grothendieck sites](c:grothendieck-site) is a dense subsite when it is locally full and locally faithful, every object of $D$ has a [covering sieve](c:covering-sieve) of arrows that factor through objects $G(c)$, and a sieve on $c$ covers exactly when its pushforward along $G$ covers $G(c)$. Then restriction along $G$ is an [equivalence](c:equivalence) between the category of [sheaves](c:sheaf) on $D$ and the category of sheaves on $C$.
examples: In $\mathrm{Open}(X)$, the full subcategory on a basis of the topology, with the induced topology, is a dense subsite, so sheaves on $X$ are the same as sheaves on the basis.
The affine open subschemes form a dense subsite of the Zariski site of a scheme.
The cartesian spaces $\mathbb{R}^n$ form a dense subsite of the site of smooth manifolds with the open cover topology.

Non-example: in $\mathrm{Open}(\mathbb{R})$, the full subcategory on the single object $\mathbb{R}$ is not a dense subsite, because an open set $U\ne\mathbb{R}$ receives no arrow from $\mathbb{R}$ and so has no covering sieve built from it.

reminder: The first derivative of a reduced homotopy functor $F$ is the spectrum with $n$th space $F(S^n)$, which describes the best linear approximation of $F$.
definition: Let $F$ be a reduced homotopy functor from pointed spaces to pointed spaces, so $F$ preserves weak equivalences and $F(\ast)\simeq\ast$. Its first (Goodwillie) derivative $\partial_1F$ is the [spectrum](c:sequential-spectrum) with $n$th space $F(S^n)$, and its best linear approximation is the [homotopy colimit](c:homotopy-colimit) $P_1F(X)=\mathrm{hocolim}_n\,\Omega^nF(\Sigma^nX)$ of [loop spaces](c:loop-space). The higher derivatives $\partial_nF$ are spectra with an action of the symmetric group, defined from the cross effects of $F$.
examples: For the identity functor on pointed spaces, $P_1\mathrm{Id}(X)=\Omega^\infty\Sigma^\infty X$ and $\partial_1\mathrm{Id}$ is the [sphere spectrum](c:sphere-spectrum).
For $F(X)=\Omega^\infty(E\wedge X)$ with $E$ a spectrum, $F$ is already linear and $\partial_1F=E$.
For $F(X)=X\wedge X$ the first derivative is trivial, because $F$ is homogeneous of degree $2$.
Non-example: a constant functor with a non-contractible value $Y$ is not reduced, because $F(\ast)=Y\not\simeq\ast$.

steps: Take $F=\mathrm{Id}$, the identity functor on pointed spaces, which is a reduced homotopy functor.
Its linear approximation is $\mathrm{hocolim}_n\,\Omega^n\Sigma^nX=\Omega^\infty\Sigma^\infty X$.
Hence its first derivative is the spectrum with $n$th space $S^n$, the sphere spectrum.
This is the first term of the [derivative of the identity functor](c:goodwillie-derivative-of-the-identity-functor).
links.why: It shows that the derivative of the identity is one computed instance of the derivative of a functor.

reminder: A presheaf with values in higher categories satisfies descent when its value on each object is the limit of its values on any cover.
definition: Let $F$ be a [presheaf](c:presheaf) on a [Grothendieck site](c:grothendieck-site) with values in a higher category. The presheaf $F$ satisfies descent when, for every [covering sieve](c:covering-sieve) $S$ on an object $U$, the canonical map $F(U)\to\lim_{(V\to U)\in S}F(V)$ is an equivalence, where the limit is a homotopy limit. The presheaves that satisfy descent are the [infinity-stacks](c:infinity-stack), and for set-valued presheaves descent is the [sheaf](c:sheaf) condition.
examples: A set-valued presheaf satisfies descent exactly when it is a sheaf, because the limit over a sieve is the set of compatible families.
The presheaf of groupoids that sends $U$ to the groupoid of vector bundles on $U$ satisfies descent, because bundles and isomorphisms glue along covers.
For a faithfully flat cover $\mathrm{Spec}\,B\to\mathrm{Spec}\,A$, quasi-coherent modules satisfy descent.
Non-example: the presheaf that sends an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}$ to the bounded functions on $U$ fails descent, because a function bounded on each member of a cover need not be bounded.

steps: Start with a set-valued presheaf $F$ and view each set as a discrete category.
The limit of $F$ over a covering sieve $S$ is the set of families $(s_V)$ that agree on overlaps.
Descent for $F$ says that $F(U)\to\lim F(V)$ is a bijection for every covering sieve.
This is the [sheaf](c:sheaf) condition: compatible families glue in a unique way.
links.why: It shows that descent is the sheaf condition with the set of compatible families replaced by a homotopy limit.

reminder: A differential algebra is an associative algebra with a derivation, a linear map that obeys the Leibniz rule.
definition: A differential algebra over a field $k$ is an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) $A$ over $k$ with a [derivation](c:derivation) $d:A\to A$, that is, a $k$-linear map with $d(ab)=d(a)b+a\,d(b)$. Some authors also require $d\circ d=0$.
examples: The polynomial ring $(k[x],d/dx)$ is a differential algebra, and so is the field $\mathbb{C}(x)$ of rational functions with $d/dx$.
The algebra $C^\infty(M)$ of smooth functions on a manifold, with a vector field acting as the derivation, is a differential algebra.
Non-example: the shift $\sigma f(x)=f(x+1)$ on $\mathbb{C}[x]$ is not a derivation, because $\sigma(fg)=\sigma(f)\sigma(g)$ and not $\sigma(f)g+f\sigma(g)$.

steps: Let $(A,d)$ be a differential algebra.
Forget $d$ and keep the sum and the product.
The remaining structure is an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra).
So a differential algebra is an associative algebra together with one extra operator $d$ that obeys the Leibniz rule.
links.why: It shows that a differential algebra is an associative algebra with one extra operation, the derivation.

reminder: A differential ideal is an ideal that the derivation maps into itself.
definition: Let $(A,d)$ be a [differential algebra](c:differential-algebra). A differential ideal is an [ideal](c:ideal) $I\subseteq A$ with $d(I)\subseteq I$. Then $d$ induces a derivation on the quotient $A/I$.
examples: In $(k[x,y],\partial_x)$ the ideal $(y)$ is a differential ideal, because $\partial_x(yf)=y\,\partial_xf$.
The kernel of a homomorphism of differential algebras is a differential ideal.
Non-example: in $(k[x],d/dx)$ the ideal $(x)$ is not a differential ideal, because $d(x)=1$ is not in $(x)$.

steps: Take a differential ideal $I$ of $(A,d)$.
Forget $d$: the set $I$ is closed under addition and under multiplication by elements of $A$, so it is an [ideal](c:ideal) of $A$.
The special case adds the condition $d(I)\subseteq I$.
links.why: It shows that a differential ideal is an ideal that also respects the derivation, so the quotient stays a differential algebra.

reminder: A dispersion relation gives the frequency of a plane wave as a function of its wavelength or wavenumber.
definition: A dispersion relation is the relation $\omega=\omega(k)$ between the angular frequency $\omega$ and the wavenumber $k=2\pi/\lambda$ of the [plane waves](c:plane-wave) $e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$ that solve a given linear equation. Substitution of a plane wave into the equation gives the relation. In scattering theory the name also covers integral formulas that connect the real part and the imaginary part of an analytic amplitude.
examples: Light in vacuum has $\omega=ck$, so all waves travel with speed $c$.
The free Schrödinger equation has $\omega=\hbar k^2/(2m)$, so longer waves travel more slowly than shorter waves.
Deep water waves satisfy $\omega=\sqrt{gk}$.
Non-example: the [wave equation](c:wave-equation) $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ is not a dispersion relation, but a plane wave in it gives one, $\omega^2=c^2k^2$.

reminder: A displayed category over a category $C$ assigns to each object and morphism of $C$ the objects and morphisms that lie over it.
definition: A displayed category $D$ over a [category](c:category) $C$ has a collection $D_c$ of objects over each object $c$ of $C$, and a set $\mathrm{Hom}_f(x,y)$ of morphisms over each morphism $f:c\to c'$ of $C$, for $x\in D_c$ and $y\in D_{c'}$. It has identities over identities and composition over composition, which satisfy the unit and associativity laws. Its total category has the pairs $(c,x)$ as objects and comes with a [functor](c:functor) to $C$.
examples: Over $\mathbf{Set}$, let $D_S=S$ and let $\mathrm{Hom}_f(s,t)$ be a point if $f(s)=t$ and empty otherwise; the total category is the category of pointed sets.
Over $\mathbf{Set}$, let $D_S$ be the monoid structures on $S$ and let $\mathrm{Hom}_f(m,m')$ be a point when $f$ is a homomorphism; the total category is the category of monoids.
A functor $F:E\to C$ gives a displayed category over $C$ whose objects over $c$ are the objects of the [fiber](c:fiber) $F^{-1}(c)$.
Non-example: a family of sets $\mathrm{Hom}_f(x,y)$ with no composition maps $\mathrm{Hom}_g(y,z)\times\mathrm{Hom}_f(x,y)\to\mathrm{Hom}_{gf}(x,z)$ is not a displayed category.

steps: Let $F:C\to\mathbf{Cat}$ be a functor.
Put $D_c=\mathrm{Ob}\,F(c)$.
For $f:c\to c'$, $x\in D_c$ and $y\in D_{c'}$, let $\mathrm{Hom}_f(x,y)=\mathrm{Hom}_{F(c')}(F(f)x,y)$.
Identities and composition come from the functoriality of $F$, and the total category is the [Grothendieck construction](c:grothendieck-construction) of $F$.
links.why: It shows that a displayed category is the general form of the data that the Grothendieck construction builds from a functor into Cat.

reminder: An abelian group is divisible when every element is $n$ times some element, for every positive integer $n$.
definition: An [abelian group](c:abelian-group) $G$, written additively, is divisible when for every $g\in G$ and every positive [integer](c:integer) $n$ there is $h\in G$ with $nh=g$. Equivalently, the map $h\mapsto nh$ is a [surjection](c:surjection) $G\to G$ for every positive $n$.
examples: The groups $\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ with addition are divisible, and so is $\mathbb{R}/\mathbb{Z}$.
The group $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ and the [Prüfer group](c:prufer-group) $\mathbb{Z}(p^\infty)$ are divisible torsion groups.
The multiplicative group $\mathbb{C}^\times$ is divisible, because every nonzero complex number has an $n$th root.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}$ is not divisible, because $1$ is not twice any integer, and no nonzero finite abelian group is divisible.

steps: Let $V$ be a [rational vector space](c:rational-vector-space) and view $(V,+)$ as an abelian group.
For $v\in V$ and $n\ge1$, put $h=\tfrac1n v$.
Then $nh=v$.
So the additive group of every rational vector space is a divisible group.
links.why: It shows that divisible groups include all rational vector spaces, and that divisible torsion groups add to them.

definition:
For [simplicial abelian groups](c:simplicial-abelian-group) $A$ and $B$, let $N$ be the normalized chains, that is, the [Moore complex](c:moore-complex), and let $A\otimes B$ be the simplicial abelian group with $(A\otimes B)_n=A_n\otimes B_n$. examples: In bidegree $(0,0)$ the map is the identity $a\otimes b\mapsto a\otimes b$.
In bidegree $(1,1)$ it sends $a\otimes b$ to a signed sum of two terms, $s_0a\otimes s_1b$ and $s_1a\otimes s_0b$, with opposite signs.

links.why: It shows that the Eilenberg-Zilber map is natural in both variables, which is why it makes the normalized chains a lax monoidal functor.

reminder: An open set engulfs a compact set when some ambient isotopy of the manifold moves the compact set into the open set.
definition: Let $M$ be a [manifold](c:manifold), $U\subseteq M$ an open set and $K\subseteq M$ a [compact](c:compact-space) set. Then $U$ engulfs $K$ when there is an ambient [isotopy](c:isotopy) $h_t$ of $M$ with compact support such that $K\subseteq h_1(U)$. Engulfing theorems, such as the Stallings-Zeeman theorem, give conditions under which this happens in a [piecewise linear manifold](c:piecewise-linear-manifold) of dimension at least $5$.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}^n$ an open ball engulfs every compact set: a compactly supported isotopy expands the ball past the set.
If $K$ is a single point, every nonempty open set $U$ of a connected manifold engulfs $K$, because an isotopy moves a point of $U$ to $K$.
Non-example: in the circle $S^1$, an open arc $U$ does not engulf $K=S^1$, because every image $h_1(U)$ is an open arc and so cannot contain $S^1$.

reminder: Two closed $G$-manifolds are equivariantly cobordant when together they form the boundary of a compact $G$-manifold.
definition: Let $G$ be a [compact Lie group](c:compact-lie-group). Two closed [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ and $N$ with a smooth [action](c:group-action) of $G$ are equivariantly [cobordant](c:cobordism) when there is a compact smooth $G$-manifold $W$ with boundary $M\sqcup N$, as $G$-manifolds. The classes under disjoint union form the unoriented equivariant cobordism group.
examples: For the trivial group $G=1$ this is ordinary unoriented cobordism.
The sphere $S^n$ with the reflection $x_0\mapsto-x_0$ is null-cobordant, because it bounds the disc $D^{n+1}$ with the same reflection.
Free $G$-manifolds up to free equivariant cobordism correspond to cobordism classes of their orbit spaces over $BG$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{R}P^2$ with the trivial $G$-action is not null-cobordant, because forgetting the action gives a nonzero class in unoriented cobordism.

steps: Take $G$ to be the trivial group.
A $G$-manifold is then an ordinary manifold, because the action is trivial.
A $G$-equivariant cobordism is an ordinary cobordism.
So equivariant cobordism for the trivial group is ordinary [cobordism](c:cobordism).
links.why: It shows that equivariant cobordism extends ordinary cobordism by carrying a group action through every manifold and every cobordism.

reminder: Equivariant cohomotopy classifies $G$-equivariant maps from a $G$-space to a representation sphere up to equivariant homotopy.
definition: Let $G$ be a [compact Lie group](c:compact-lie-group), $V$ a real [group representation](c:group-representation) of $G$, and $S^V$ its [representation sphere](c:representation-sphere), the one-point compactification of $V$ with the induced action of $G$. The equivariant cohomotopy set $\pi^V_G(X)$ of a $G$-space $X$ is the set of $G$-equivariant homotopy classes of $G$-maps $X\to S^V$. For trivial $G$ and $V=\mathbb{R}^n$ it is [cohomotopy](c:cohomotopy).
examples: For trivial $G$ and $V=\mathbb{R}^n$, $\pi^n(X)=[X,S^n]$, and for an $n$-dimensional CW complex $X$ this is $H^n(X;\mathbb{Z})$ by the Hopf theorem.
Restriction to the trivial subgroup forgets equivariance and gives an ordinary cohomotopy class of $X$ with values in $S^{\dim V}$.
Non-example: equivariant cohomology $H^n_G(X)$ is not equivariant cohomotopy, because it is represented by Eilenberg-MacLane spaces and not by representation spheres.

steps: Take $G$ to be the trivial group.
A representation $V$ is then a real vector space $\mathbb{R}^n$, and $S^V=S^n$.
A $G$-map is an ordinary map, and a $G$-homotopy is an ordinary homotopy.
So $\pi^V_G(X)=[X,S^n]$, which is the [cohomotopy](c:cohomotopy) set of $X$.
links.why: It shows that equivariant cohomotopy is cohomotopy with a group acting on the space and on the sphere.
